items.abstract: Rapid digitalization in higher education, combined with the need for universities to operate under geographically distributed and relocated conditions, highlights a crucial shift from rigid hierarchical management to flexible, decentralized systems. This paper substantiates the architecture of decentralized university management models driven by multi-agent systems and large language models (LLMs), presenting its architectural justification and functional implementation within a higher education institution. The study details theoretical foundations of utilizing multi-agent systems, orchestration protocols, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and vector databases to optimize university workflows under conditions of limited observability and distributed IT infrastructure. The methodology rests on a two-tier multi-agent architecture, where dynamic request routing is achieved through a hierarchical orchestration model using AgentSpec formal specifications, while action consistency is maintained by a central algorithmic coordinator. Findings indicate that deploying a standalone autonomous agent for each of the university’s 24 departments is inefficient due to risks of algorithmic conflicts, redundant queries to the vector knowledge base, increased LLM hallucination rates, and context window constraints. To address these limitations, a coordinated multi-agent architecture was implemented at Kherson State University. This framework consolidates operations into five core macro-agents—academic affairs, administrative management, knowledge management, educational quality assurance, and communications—managed by a Central Orchestrator routing queries, controlling access privileges, and synthesizing analytical outputs. The paper identifies key organizational and technological hurdles, focusing on maintaining high levels of trust, decision verification, and role-based access control during delegation. Finally, it outlines the roadmap for evolving this framework into a university digital twin capable of predictive modeling and automated process support. These findings offer practical value for higher education institutions deploying digital ecosystems under human resource, infrastructural, and security constraints.

items.abstract: Recent years have witnessed rapid advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) models such as ChatGPT and Gemini, opening new prospects for supporting the educational process. This study aims to measure the effectiveness of generative AI models in improving university students' academic writing skills, using a quasi-experimental design with experimental and control groups (N = 60 second-year students of the Faculty of Education, randomly assigned to the two groups). The experimental group received a six-week training program that integrated generative AI as a writing assistant across brainstorming, drafting, language revision, and referencing, while the control group followed traditional instruction. An academic writing skills test and an observation checklist were used as instruments. The study hypothesizes statistically significant differences (α = 0.05) favoring the experimental group in thesis clarity, idea organization, linguistic accuracy, and academic referencing, alongside positive attitudes toward AI as a supportive tool rather than a substitute for thinking. In addition, an exploratory descriptive survey of 87 university students found that 93.1% had previously used generative AI tools for academic writing, 95.4% supported clear university policies governing their use, and 72.4% reported concern about over-reliance on them. The study recommends training faculty members to integrate generative AI tools into academic writing courses and establishing an ethical charter to govern their use.

items.abstract: Traditional circuit breakers provide protection against overcurrent and short-circuit conditions but have no inherent provision for remote supervision, demand awareness or intelligent load management. This paper introduces the design, implementation and experimental testing of a smart circuit breaker that combines independent electrical protection, hybrid Global System for Mobile communication (GSM)–Internet of Things (IoT) connectivity, and an energy optimization layer based on artificial intelligence (AI). An edge controller measures voltage, current, active power and energy in real time and publishes telemetry through a Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) link or, when Internet connectivity is lost, through the GSM short-message service (SMS). A hybrid Long Short-Term Memory–Extreme Gradient Boosting (LSTM–XGBoost) model forecasts short-term demand, and a weighted objective function schedules deferrable loads to minimize electricity cost and peak demand while satisfying circuit-capacity and user-priority constraints. Software and communication functions never substitute for hardware protection; a certified miniature circuit breaker (MCB) remains the primary fault-interruption device. the prototype measured the electrical quantities with a maximum loaded-condition deviation of 0.76% from the calibrated reference values; the forecaster achieved an RMSE of 0.083 kW and a coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.9899; and the hybrid channel maintained a 97.1% command-success rate during controlled Internet-outage trials, whereas the IoT-only channel recorded 0%. Compared with conventional operation, the AI-driven strategy reduced peak demand by 39.6% and electricity cost by 8.0%, whereas total energy consumption decreased by only 3.0%, indicating that its main advantage is peak-demand reduction rather than energy reduction. These findings indicate the feasibility of a deployable device that combines protection, resilient communication and predictive energy management.
